newsitem.title: USA: Clinton to propose 30 pct capital gains exclusion.
newsitem.headline: Clinton to propose 30 pct capital gains exclusion.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Monday will propose giving investors a 30 percent tax exclusion on capital gains instead of cutting the capital gains tax rate outright as Republicans advocate, a White House official said.
The proposal, due to be unveiled at 9:30 EDT (1330 GMT), is Democrat Clinton's response to the tax bills passed last week by the Republican-controlled House of Representatives and Senate.

The Congress is in the process of writing the detailed tax and spending bills needed to enact the balanced-budget agreement that Clinton and the Republicans hammered out in May and that aims to eliminate the federal budget deficit by 2002.
While some of the elements that Clinton will describe on Monday clearly represent a step in the Republicans' direction, others are unlikely to find much support among them.

On capital gains, Clinton's proposal was designed to target tax cuts to benefit middle income citizens rather than the wealthy, said the official, who asked not to be named. It is likely to meet stiff resistance from Republicans, who want to cut the capital gains tax rate to 20 percent from 28 percent at present.

Under the administration plan, a citizen who made a $100 capital gain would be allowed to exclude 30 percent of the gain, or $30, from taxation. He or she would then pay tax at whatever rate was stipulated by their income tax bracket.

As a result, the official said, the capital gains tax rate for those who pay the highest marginal tax rate of 39.6 percent would effectively be cut to 27.8 percent. Individuals would have to hold investments for one year to qualify for the exclusion.
Those now in the 28-percent income-tax bracket would see their capital gains tax rate effectively cut to 19.6 percent, and those in the 15-percent bracket to 10.5 percent, he added.

"This is a way of structuring it so more of the benefits go to middle income taxpayers," said the official. "It's obvious that for the wealthiest taxpayers this would not be nearly as generous as the House and Senate bills."
At present, capital gains on investments held for more than one year are taxed at a flat 28 percent rate.
The House and Senate bills would cut this to 20 percent, with the House bill permitting investors to subtract the effects of inflation in calculating gains, a process known as indexing.
The White House official said that Clinton continues to strongly oppose indexing capital gains.

He said the proposals Clinton will unveil on Monday would be consistent with the balanced budget plan, offering a net tax cut of $85 billion over five years. Over 10 years, the net tax cut would amount to $241 billion.
Other elements of the tax proposals that Clinton was to unveil include a tax credit for children under the age of 17 through the year 2002 and under the age of 19 after that.
The child tax credit would be $400 in fiscal year 1998, which begins October 1, 1997, rising to $500 in fiscal 1999 and indexed for inflation thereafter, the official said.

In offering such a credit, Clinton is taking a step toward the Republicans. The president had originally wanted to offer the credit only to children under the age of 13 and he had phased in the full $500 over several years.
Another element of Clinton's plan would be to rejig his "Hope Scholarships" proposal that was originally a straight $1,500 tax credit to pay for college tuition.

The White House official said Clinton's new plan would offer a straight $1,000 tax credit to pay for the first $1,000 of college tuition and a 50 percent tax credit for up to the next $1,000. The overall credit, worth up to $1,500, would be available for the first two years of college.
The official said Clinton would abandon his plan for a $10,000 tax deduction for education, instead offering a newly designed tax credit for the third and fourth years of college.
This would entail a 20-percent tax credit on the first $5,000 in college tuition up to the year 2000, after which the 20 percent credit could be applied to up to the first $10,000.

Finally, the official said Clinton would propose a 20 cent per pack rise in cigarette taxes, earmarking the proceeds for a trust fund devoted to children's health care, public health and other programmes.
